subject: Biotechnology
title: The First Gene Therapy Trial
description: One-minute skill: The First Gene Therapy Trial.

hook.text: In 1990, a four-year-old girl received the first approved gene therapy — for a deadly immune deficiency.

buildup.text: Ashanti DeSilva had ADA-SCID — her immune cells could not fight infections because one gene was broken.

discovery.text: Doctors extracted her white blood cells, inserted a working ADA gene, and returned them — her immunity improved.

twist.text: The effect was temporary — the corrected cells died off and she still needed enzyme replacement therapy.

climax.text: The trial proved gene therapy was possible — but permanent cures would need better vectors and techniques.

punchline.text: The first gene therapy patient is still alive — proof of concept earned.

quiz.question: Why was the first gene therapy only temporarily effective?
options: The patient's immune system destroyed the therapeutic gene
The corrected cells eventually died off without permanent genomic integration
The inserted gene mutated and stopped functioning

details.summary: The first approved human gene therapy trial in 1990 treated Ashanti DeSilva, a four-year-old with severe combined immunodeficiency, by inserting the adenosine deaminase gene into her T cells using a retroviral vector.
details.whyItMatters: Ashanti DeSilva's treatment demonstrated that genetic diseases could be treated by delivering functional genes to patients. Despite modest efficacy, the trial launched the clinical gene therapy era and established the framework for all subsequent
takeaways: The 1990 trial treated a child with severe combined immunodeficiency
A retroviral vector delivered the missing ADA gene to extracted T cells
The treatment improved immune function but required ongoing enzyme replacement

faq.question: Did the first gene therapy trial cure the patient?
faq.answer: Not completely. Ashanti DeSilva showed improved T cell function and attended school normally but continued receiving PEG-ADA enzyme replacement. The retrovirally modified T cells persisted for years but the treatment was supplementary rather than curative. It proved the concept was feasible.

faq.question: Why did it take decades after the first trial for gene therapy to succeed?
faq.answer: Early retroviral vectors integrated randomly, causing leukemia in some patients. The Jesse Gelsinger death in 1999 triggered a funding and regulatory crisis. Safer AAV vectors, improved gene transfer methods, and better patient selection were needed before clinical success became reliable.
